The tray side walls are spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages.

It includes a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages. Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover.

The lid carries a depending indexing rib. As the lid closes, the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell so that the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport.

A removable absorbent wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the product tray. Openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel. A pull tab on the wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, allowing the wick to be replaced without opening a phase-change cassette.

The shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator does not control airflow.

For use, conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame, products are placed in the tray, the thermal module is placed above the tray, and the lid is closed to register and retain the module. The disclosed essential relationship is the registered passive circulation path around the removable tray and opposed cassettes, combined with lid-driven registration of the thermal module. input.content:
Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.

Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.

Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.

Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.

There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.

A passive cold-chain carrier is disclosed in which the closing of the lid, rather than the care of the packer, establishes the circulation path.

In one aspect, the carrier includes an insulated outer shell having a floor and side walls, a product tray removably received in the outer shell, a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, and an insulated lid. The product tray is supported above the floor by tray feet so that a lower return passage remains between the product tray and the floor, and the tray side walls are spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell to form two side supply passages. The thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings. The insulated lid carries a depending indexing rib positioned to enter a mating channel of the spacer frame as the lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.

In the registered position the shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the lid cooperate to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the circulation is driven by the density difference between the air warmed in the product region and the air cooled along the cassette faces.

The technical effect of lid-driven registration is that the alignment on which the circulation path depends is created by an act the packer cannot omit. The thermal module may be dropped into the shell approximately, offset or skewed, and the descending indexing rib entering the mating channel translates the module into the position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The seal made by a compressible lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell occurs after registration, so the carrier is not closed against a module that is still out of position. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, so that the registered module is held down against the product tray and cannot lift away from it under the vibration and inversion of transport.

In a further aspect, a shallow condensate channel extends around the product tray and receives a removable absorbent wick. Discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts deliver condensate that forms on the cassettes into the condensate channel. A pull tab on the absorbent wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, so the wick is replaced without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service.

In a further aspect, the outer shell carries a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside the carrier. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position, and the indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again, being reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator therefore reports the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends, survives recovery of the cassette, and requires no battery. The exposure indicator does not control airflow, so the circulation path is unaffected by whether the indicator has tripped.

In a further aspect, a method includes fitting conditioned phase-change cassettes to the spacer frame, placing product in the product tray, placing the product tray in the outer shell, placing the thermal module above the product tray, and closing the insulated lid so that the depending indexing rib enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into the registered position, whereafter air circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover.

The features summarised above may be used together or separately, and the summary is not a statement of the scope of the claims.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60 and, in some implementations, the product tray 20 and the spacer frame 42 described below are formed of thermally insulating material such as moulded expanded polymer, a vacuum insulated panel assembly, a rigid polyurethane foam core within a moulded skin, or a combination of these. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being liftable out of the outer shell 10 for loading, cleaning and reconditioning.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12. The tray feet 22 may be integrally moulded projections, separate ribs, or a pedestal frame, and are of sufficient number and footprint to carry a loaded tray without collapsing the lower return passage 24.

Referring also to FIG. 4, the tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the product region and into the lower return passage 24. The perforations 30 may be formed in a lower portion of the tray side walls 26, in the bottom wall of the product tray 20, or in both, and may be round holes, slots, or a louvered pattern. In each case the perforations 30 are distributed along the length of the product tray 20 so that air delivered by the side supply passages 28 enters the product region along that length rather than at a single point.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette is a sealed rigid container charged with a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42 so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload can be fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50 located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50. The spacer frame 42 holds the phase-change cassettes clear of the product tray 20, so that goods in the product region are not in contact with a cassette surface and are cooled by the circulating air rather than by direct contact.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42. In some implementations the mating channel 56 has side surfaces that converge downward, so that engagement of a rib entering the mating channel from above cams the spacer frame 42 horizontally rather than simply resting in the channel. The resilient feet 58 may be elastomeric pads, moulded spring tabs, or compressible polymer blocks.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. Referring to FIG. 3, as the insulated lid 60 is closed the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 need only be dropped into the outer shell 10 approximately, and may be set down offset or skewed within the clearance available to it. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is then created by closing the lid, which is an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 project inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10 beneath the resilient feet 58, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42 against the ledges 18, as seen in FIG. 3. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. Retention by compression of resilient members accommodates the tolerance stack of moulded insulating parts, and maintains a downward holding force as the carrier is jolted or inverted, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the confronting inner faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces. Each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: the cooled air is produced at the top of the carrier and is given a continuous downward path of its own along the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, while the warmed air is given a continuous upward path through the product region to the central inlet opening 48, and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cold stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warm stream, and the payload is swept along its length rather than chilled at the surface nearest a refrigerant mass. The lower return passage 24 also keeps the coldest returning air off the goods until it has mixed, so that goods at the bottom of the product tray 20 are not driven below the temperature band.

Condensate management

Referring to FIG. 4, a condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76 at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior. The absorbent wick 72 may be a cellulose or polymer fibre strip, a superabsorbent polymer sleeve, or a moulded absorbent ring shaped to the condensate channel 70.

Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 5, the outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes a body received in the outer shell 10, an indicator stem 82 movable in the body between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60 and, in some implementations, the product tray 20 and the spacer frame 42 described below are formed of thermally insulating material such as moulded expanded polymer, a vacuum insulated panel assembly, a rigid polyurethane foam core within a moulded skin, or a combination of these. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being liftable out of the outer shell 10 for loading, cleaning and reconditioning.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12. The tray feet 22 may be integrally moulded projections, separate ribs, or a pedestal frame, and are of sufficient number and footprint to carry a loaded tray without collapsing the lower return passage 24.

Referring also to FIG. 4, the tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the product region and into the lower return passage 24. The perforations 30 may be formed in a lower portion of the tray side walls 26, in the bottom wall of the product tray 20, or in both, and may be round holes, slots, or a louvered pattern. In each case the perforations 30 are distributed along the length of the product tray 20 so that air delivered by the side supply passages 28 enters the product region along that length rather than at a single point.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette is a sealed rigid container charged with a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42 so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload can be fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50 located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50. The spacer frame 42 holds the phase-change cassettes clear of the product tray 20, so that goods in the product region are not in contact with a cassette surface and are cooled by the circulating air rather than by direct contact.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42. In some implementations the mating channel 56 has side surfaces that converge downward, so that engagement of a rib entering the mating channel from above cams the spacer frame 42 horizontally rather than simply resting in the channel. The resilient feet 58 may be elastomeric pads, moulded spring tabs, or compressible polymer blocks.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. Referring to FIG. 3, as the insulated lid 60 is closed the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 need only be dropped into the outer shell 10 approximately, and may be set down offset or skewed within the clearance available to it. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is then created by closing the lid, which is an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 project inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10 beneath the resilient feet 58, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42 against the ledges 18, as seen in FIG. 3. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. Retention by compression of resilient members accommodates the tolerance stack of moulded insulating parts, and maintains a downward holding force as the carrier is jolted or inverted, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the confronting inner faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces. Each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cold stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warm stream, and the payload is swept along its length rather than chilled at the surface nearest a refrigerant mass. The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. The exposed position is a latched position. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60 and, in some implementations, the product tray 20 and the spacer frame 42 described below are formed of thermally insulating material such as moulded expanded polymer, a vacuum insulated panel assembly, a rigid polyurethane foam core within a moulded skin, or a combination of these. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being liftable out of the outer shell 10 for loading, cleaning and reconditioning.

+Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material such as moulded expanded polymer, a vacuum insulated panel assembly, a rigid polyurethane foam core within a moulded skin, or a combination of these. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being liftable out of the outer shell 10 for loading, cleaning and reconditioning.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12. The tray feet 22 may be integrally moulded projections, separate ribs, or a pedestal frame, and are of sufficient number and footprint to carry a loaded tray without collapsing the lower return passage 24.

lines: Registration and retention by the lid

-The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. Referring to FIG. 3, as the insulated lid 60 is closed the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

+The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 need only be dropped into the outer shell 10 approximately, and may be set down offset or skewed within the clearance available to it. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is then created by closing the lid, which is an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

lines: Condensate management

-Referring to FIG. 4, a condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76 at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

+A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76 at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 4. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior. The absorbent wick 72 may be a cellulose or polymer fibre strip, a superabsorbent polymer sleeve, or a moulded absorbent ring shaped to the condensate channel 70.

input.content:
1. A passive cold-chain carrier comprising:

an insulated outer shell having a floor, side walls and an upper edge;

a product tray removably received in the outer shell, the product tray having a bottom wall, tray side walls, perforations, and tray feet standing on the floor so that the product tray is supported above the floor and a lower return passage remains between the bottom wall and the floor, the tray side walls being spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell so that two side supply passages are formed;

a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, the thermal module comprising a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, and a mating channel; and

an insulated lid closable on the upper edge of the outer shell and carrying a depending indexing rib positioned to enter the mating channel as the insulated lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages;

the carrier being free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the outer shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the insulated lid cooperating in the registered position to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through the perforations, and returns through the lower return passage.

2. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the spacer frame carries resilient feet, the side walls of the outer shell have ledges beneath the resilient feet, and closure of the insulated lid presses the resilient feet against the ledges so that the thermal module is held down against lifting away from the product tray.

3. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a compressible lid gasket carried by the insulated lid and arranged to seal against the upper edge of the outer shell after the depending indexing rib has shifted the thermal module into the registered position.

4. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 3, wherein the compressible lid gasket extends around an underside of the insulated lid outboard of the depending indexing rib.

5. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the two opposed phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame with an inner face of a first phase-change cassette confronting an inner face of a second phase-change cassette across a central space, the central inlet opening opens downward into the central space, and each guide duct lies outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes.

6. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame, and the spacer frame holds the phase-change cassettes clear of the product tray so that goods in the product region are cooled by air of the circulation path rather than by contact with a phase-change cassette.

7. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the perforations are formed in a lower portion of the tray side walls and are distributed along a length of the product tray.

8. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a condensate channel extending around the product tray at a lower region of the outer shell beneath the side supply passages, and a removable absorbent wick lying in the condensate channel.

9. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 8, wherein the guide ducts have discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, the discharge openings discharging condensate into the condensate channel.

10. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 8, wherein the absorbent wick carries a pull tab that remains accessible when the product tray is removed from the outer shell, so that the absorbent wick is replaceable without opening a phase-change cassette.

11. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a mechanical exposure indicator carried by the outer shell and visible from outside the carrier, the mechanical exposure indicator comprising an indicator stem thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes, a temperature-responsive latch retaining the indicator stem in a stowed position, and a spring biasing the indicator stem toward an exposed position, the temperature-responsive latch releasing the indicator stem when said one of the phase-change cassettes softens.

12. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 11, wherein the exposed position is a latched position in which the mechanical exposure indicator retains the indicator stem after said one of the phase-change cassettes has cooled again, the mechanical exposure indicator being resettable manually only after the carrier is opened.

13. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 11, wherein the mechanical exposure indicator does not control airflow, the circulation path being the same whether or not the indicator stem stands in the exposed position.

14. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 11, wherein an inner end region of the indicator stem lies in conductive contact with said one of the phase-change cassettes when the thermal module is in the registered position.

15. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the depending indexing rib meets the mating channel while the insulated lid is spaced above the upper edge of the outer shell, and remaining closing travel of the insulated lid translates the spacer frame horizontally into the registered position.

16. A thermal module for a passive cold-chain carrier having an insulated outer shell, a product tray defining side supply passages with side walls of the outer shell, and an insulated lid carrying a depending indexing rib, the thermal module comprising:

a rigid spacer frame sized to be removably received in the outer shell above the product tray; and

two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame;

the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening through which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the spacer frame, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes and receiving air that has divided along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, and a mating channel positioned to be entered by the depending indexing rib as the insulated lid closes so that the thermal module is shifted into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.

17. The thermal module of claim 16, further comprising resilient feet at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame, the resilient feet being positioned to be pressed against ledges of the outer shell by closure of the insulated lid so that the thermal module is held down against the product tray.

18. The thermal module of claim 16, wherein the mating channel opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame and has side surfaces that converge downward.

19. The thermal module of claim 16, wherein the guide ducts have discharge openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts, the discharge openings being positioned to discharge condensate formed on the phase-change cassettes into a condensate channel of the outer shell.

20. A method of transporting temperature-sensitive goods, the method comprising:

fitting two conditioned phase-change cassettes to a rigid spacer frame of a thermal module, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, and a mating channel;

placing the goods in a product tray and placing the product tray in an insulated outer shell so that tray feet of the product tray stand on a floor of the outer shell, leaving a lower return passage between the product tray and the floor and two side supply passages between tray side walls of the product tray and side walls of the outer shell;

placing the thermal module in the outer shell above the product tray;

closing an insulated lid on an upper edge of the outer shell so that a depending indexing rib carried by the insulated lid enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages; and

thereafter transporting the goods while air circulates, without operation of any powered air mover, along a circulation path in which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage.

21. The method of claim 20, wherein closing the insulated lid further presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, retaining the thermal module against lifting away from the product tray during the transporting, and compresses a lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell after the thermal module has been shifted into the registered position.

22. The method of claim 20, further comprising, after the transporting, opening the insulated lid, removing the product tray from the outer shell, and drawing a removable absorbent wick out of a condensate channel of the outer shell by a pull tab of the absorbent wick without opening a phase-change cassette.

23. The method of claim 20, further comprising reading, from outside the outer shell, a mechanical exposure indicator having an indicator stem thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes, the indicator stem having been moved by a spring to a latched exposed position on release of a temperature-responsive latch by softening of said one of the phase-change cassettes and remaining in the latched exposed position after said one of the phase-change cassettes has cooled again, and resetting the mechanical exposure indicator manually after the insulated lid has been opened.

# FIG. 1

## View
A vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, seen horizontally, in plain black line work on a white background. Cut material is shown with uniform diagonal section hatching. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins on every side.

## Geometry to draw
An upright rectangular container occupies the centre of the drawing area: a thick hatched left wall body and a thick hatched right wall body of equal height, joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body that spans between them. Together these form the sectioned insulated outer shell 10, whose bottom body is the floor 12. The container is open at the top.

A thick hatched horizontal slab lies across the top ends of the left and right wall bodies and spans the full outer width of the container. This slab is the insulated lid 60 in the closed position, its underside contacting the top surfaces of both wall bodies.

Inside the container, in its lower two thirds, a sectioned open-top box is drawn with thin hatched walls: an upright left wall, an upright right wall and a horizontal bottom wall joining them, open at the top. This box is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the top surface of the floor 12, and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the inner surfaces of the left and right wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side that runs from the top of the box down to the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks stand between the underside of the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the top surface of the floor 12, one near the left end and one near the right end of the tray. These blocks are the tray feet 22. The open horizontal space between the underside of the tray bottom wall and the top surface of the floor 12, extending between and beyond the two blocks, is the lower return passage 24.

In the upper part of the container interior, between the inner surfaces of the left and right wall bodies and between the open top of the product tray 20 and the underside of the insulated lid 60, a horizontally elongated hatched body is drawn in section. This body is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks are drawn within it, spaced apart from one another and from its outboard ends, shown schematically. The hatched body is open downward at its centre between the two upright blocks, and an open vertical channel runs down through the hatched body outboard of each upright block, each channel opening downward at the lower outboard end of the body above the corresponding vertical gap beside the product tray 20.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

## Numeral targets
- 10: well inside the hatching of the left wall body of the outer shell.
- 12: well inside the hatching of the horizontal bottom body.
- 20: well inside the hatching of the left upright wall of the sectioned open-top box.
- 22: well inside the hatching of the left short block standing on the floor.
- 24: well inside the open horizontal space between the tray bottom wall and the floor.
- 40: well inside the hatching of the horizontally elongated body in the upper interior, at a point between its centre and its left end and clear of the upright blocks.
- 60: well inside the hatching of the horizontal slab at the top.
- 100: on the outer side surface of the right wall body of the container, at mid height, identifying the assembled carrier as a whole.

# FIG. 2

## View
A perspective view of the thermal module alone, removed from the carrier, seen from above and in front of the module so that the open top, the near long side and the near short end are all visible. Plain black line work on a white background, no hatching. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins on every side.

## Geometry to draw
The main body is an upright rectangular open frame, longer from left to right than it is deep from front to back, and shallower in height than it is deep. It has a near long side wall, a far long side wall, a left short end wall, a right short end wall, and a bottom panel joining the four walls. The top of the frame is open. This frame is the spacer frame 42, and the frame together with the slabs described below is the thermal module 40.

Two flat rectangular slabs stand upright inside the frame, each parallel to the long side walls and each running most of the length of the frame. The slabs are spaced apart from one another across the depth of the frame, leaving an open central gap between their confronting broad faces, and each slab is also spaced from the adjacent long side wall, leaving an open vertical channel between that slab and that wall. The slab nearer the front is the first phase-change cassette 44 and the slab nearer the back is the second phase-change cassette 46. Each slab is drawn as a plain closed rectangular box, shown schematically, its upper edge standing below the top edges of the frame walls.

In the bottom panel of the frame, within the open central gap between the two slabs, a rectangular through opening is drawn, so that the bottom panel is open there and the viewer looks down through it. This through opening is the central inlet opening 48.

lines: Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette is a sealed rigid container charged with a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42 so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload can be fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

-The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50 located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50. The spacer frame 42 holds the phase-change cassettes clear of the product tray 20, so that goods in the product region are not in contact with a cassette surface and are cooled by the circulating air rather than by direct contact.

+The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50. The spacer frame 42 holds the phase-change cassettes clear of the product tray 20, so that goods in the product region are not in contact with a cassette surface and are cooled by the circulating air rather than by direct contact.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42. The mating channel 56 and the rib that enters it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other. The resilient feet 58 may be elastomeric pads, moulded spring tabs, or compressible polymer blocks.

1	In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material such as moulded expanded polymer, a vacuum insulated panel assembly, a rigid polyurethane foam core within a moulded skin, or a combination of these. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being liftable out of the outer shell 10 for loading, cleaning and reconditioning.
6	
7	The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12. The tray feet 22 may be integrally moulded projections, separate ribs, or a pedestal frame, and are of sufficient number and footprint to carry a loaded tray without collapsing the lower return passage 24.
8	
9	The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the product region and into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4. The perforations 30 may be formed in a lower portion of the tray side walls 26, in the bottom wall of the product tray 20, or in both, and may be round holes, slots, or a louvered pattern. In each case the perforations 30 are distributed along the length of the product tray 20 so that air delivered by the side supply passages 28 enters the product region along that length rather than at a single point.
10	
11	The thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette is a sealed rigid container charged with a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42 so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload can be fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.
14	
15	The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50. The spacer frame 42 holds the phase-change cassettes clear of the product tray 20, so that goods in the product region are not in contact with a cassette surface and are cooled by the circulating air rather than by direct contact.
16	
17	The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42. The mating channel 56 and the rib that enters it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other. The resilient feet 58 may be elastomeric pads, moulded spring tabs, or compressible polymer blocks.
18	
19	Registration and retention by the lid
20	
21	The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.
22	
23	This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 need only be dropped into the outer shell 10 approximately, and may be set down offset or skewed within the clearance available to it. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is then created by closing the lid, which is an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.
24	
25	The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 project inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10 beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. Retention by compression of resilient members accommodates the tolerance stack of moulded insulating parts, and maintains a downward holding force as the carrier is jolted or inverted, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.
26	
27	The circulation path
28	
29	In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the confronting inner faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces. Each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.
30	
31	The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: the cooled air is produced at the top of the carrier and is given a continuous downward path of its own along the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, while the warmed air is given a continuous upward path through the product region to the central inlet opening 48, and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cold stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warm stream, and the payload is swept along its length rather than chilled at the surface nearest a refrigerant mass. The lower return passage 24 also keeps the coldest returning air off the goods until it has mixed, so that goods at the bottom of the product tray 20 are not driven below the temperature band.
32	
33	Condensate management
34	
35	A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76 at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 4. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.
36	
37	The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior. The absorbent wick 72 may be a cellulose or polymer fibre strip, a superabsorbent polymer sleeve, or a moulded absorbent ring shaped to the condensate channel 70.
38	
39	Mechanical exposure indicator
40	
41	Referring to FIG. 5, the outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes a body received in the outer shell 10, an indicator stem 82 movable in the body between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44, an inner end region of the indicator stem 82 lying against or in conductive contact with the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.
42	
43	The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens, that is, when the phase-change material of that cassette has passed out of the state in which it holds the payload at temperature. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10. In some implementations the exposed position is one in which an outer end portion of the indicator stem 82 projects beyond an outer surface of the outer shell 10; in others it is one in which a contrasting portion of the indicator stem 82 is presented at the outer surface.
44	
45	The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.
46	
47	The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.
48	
49	Operation
50	
51	In use, phase-change cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by the payload are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.
52	
53	Alternatives
54	
55	The number of phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42 is two in the described arrangement, the two being opposed across the central space so that each face of the rising stream is cooled symmetrically. The mating channel 56 and the depending indexing rib 62 may be interchanged in the sense that the channel may be longer than the rib or the rib longer than the channel, provided that entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 may be continuous slots along the outboard lower regions of the spacer frame 42 or a series of discrete openings, provided that they overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.
56	
57	The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.
