In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material such as moulded expanded polymer, a vacuum insulated panel assembly, a rigid polyurethane foam core within a moulded skin, or a combination of these. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being liftable out of the outer shell 10 for loading, cleaning and reconditioning.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12. The tray feet 22 may be integrally moulded projections, separate ribs, or a pedestal frame, and are of sufficient number and footprint to carry a loaded tray without collapsing the lower return passage 24.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the product region and into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4. The perforations 30 may be formed in a lower portion of the tray side walls 26, in the bottom wall of the product tray 20, or in both, and may be round holes, slots, or a louvered pattern. In each case the perforations 30 are distributed along the length of the product tray 20 so that air delivered by the side supply passages 28 enters the product region along that length rather than at a single point.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette is a sealed rigid container charged with a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42 so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload can be fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50. The spacer frame 42 holds the phase-change cassettes clear of the product tray 20, so that goods in the product region are not in contact with a cassette surface and are cooled by the circulating air rather than by direct contact.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42. The mating channel 56 and the rib that enters it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other. The resilient feet 58 may be elastomeric pads, moulded spring tabs, or compressible polymer blocks.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 need only be dropped into the outer shell 10 approximately, and may be set down offset or skewed within the clearance available to it. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is then created by closing the lid, which is an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 project inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10 beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. Retention by compression of resilient members accommodates the tolerance stack of moulded insulating parts, and maintains a downward holding force as the carrier is jolted or inverted, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the confronting inner faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces. Each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: the cooled air is produced at the top of the carrier and is given a continuous downward path of its own along the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, while the warmed air is given a continuous upward path through the product region to the central inlet opening 48, and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cold stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warm stream, and the payload is swept along its length rather than chilled at the surface nearest a refrigerant mass. The lower return passage 24 also keeps the coldest returning air off the goods until it has mixed, so that goods at the bottom of the product tray 20 are not driven below the temperature band.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76 at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 4. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior. The absorbent wick 72 may be a cellulose or polymer fibre strip, a superabsorbent polymer sleeve, or a moulded absorbent ring shaped to the condensate channel 70.

Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 5, the outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes a body received in the outer shell 10, an indicator stem 82 movable in the body between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44, an inner end region of the indicator stem 82 lying against or in conductive contact with the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens, that is, when the phase-change material of that cassette has passed out of the state in which it holds the payload at temperature. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10. In some implementations the exposed position is one in which an outer end portion of the indicator stem 82 projects beyond an outer surface of the outer shell 10; in others it is one in which a contrasting portion of the indicator stem 82 is presented at the outer surface.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, phase-change cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by the payload are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Alternatives

The number of phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42 is two in the described arrangement, the two being opposed across the central space so that each face of the rising stream is cooled symmetrically. The mating channel 56 and the depending indexing rib 62 may be interchanged in the sense that the channel may be longer than the rib or the rib longer than the channel, provided that entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 may be continuous slots along the outboard lower regions of the spacer frame 42 or a series of discrete openings, provided that they overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

# FIG. 1

## View
Vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, seen horizontally. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
An upright rectangular container occupies the centre of the drawing area: a thick hatched left wall body and a thick hatched right wall body of equal height, joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body spanning between them. These form the sectioned outer shell 10, whose bottom body is the floor 12. The container is open at the top.

A thick hatched horizontal slab lies across the top ends of both wall bodies, spanning the full outer width, its underside contacting both. This slab is the insulated lid 60, closed.

Inside the container, in its lower two thirds, a sectioned open-top box is drawn with thin hatched walls: an upright left wall, an upright right wall and a horizontal bottom wall joining them. This box is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the top surface of the floor 12, and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the inner surfaces of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side running from the top of the box down to the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks stand between the underside of the tray bottom wall and the top surface of the floor 12, one near each end of the tray. These blocks are the tray feet 22. The open horizontal space between that underside and that top surface, extending between and beyond the blocks, is the lower return passage 24.

In the upper interior, between the inner surfaces of the two wall bodies and between the open top of the product tray 20 and the underside of the insulated lid 60, a horizontally elongated hatched body is drawn in section. This body is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks are drawn within it, shown schematically, spaced from one another and from its outboard ends. The hatched body is open downward at its centre between those blocks, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening downward at the lower outboard end of the body above the vertical gap beside the product tray 20.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

- 10: well inside the hatching of the left wall body.
- 12: well inside the hatching of the horizontal bottom body.
- 20: well inside the hatching of the left upright wall of the open-top box.
- 22: well inside the left short block standing on the floor.
- 24: inside the open horizontal space between the tray bottom wall and the floor.
- 40: well inside the hatching of the elongated upper body, between its centre and its left end, clear of the upright blocks.
- 60: well inside the hatching of the horizontal slab at the top.
- 100: on the outer side surface of the right wall body at mid height, identifying the assembled carrier as a whole.

# FIG. 3

## View
Enlarged fragmentary vertical sectional view of an upper side region of the carrier, seen horizontally, with the lid closed on the top of the thermal module. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
A thick hatched upright wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area, running from an upper end down to the lower edge of the fragment, its outer surface facing left and its inner surface facing right. This is one of the side walls 14 of the sectioned outer shell. Partway down the inner surface, a hatched block projects rightward from it and has a flat upwardly facing top surface. This projection is one of the ledges 18.

Across the upper part of the drawing area lies a thick hatched horizontal closure slab, shown in section, spanning from the left edge of the fragment rightward past the middle of the drawing area, its underside facing the top end of the upright wall body.

A small hatched body of compressible material lies between the underside of the closure slab and the flat top end surface of the upright wall body, contacting both and flattened between them.

Inboard of that compressible body, a narrow rib projects downward from the underside of the closure slab as an integral part of it, extending below the level of the top end of the upright wall body. This projection is the depending indexing rib 62.

To the right of the upright wall body, spaced from its inner surface, a hatched body is drawn in section extending from beneath the closure slab down to the level of the ledge 18. This body is the sectioned spacer frame 42. Its upper edge carries an upwardly open groove whose width matches the thickness of the depending indexing rib 62 and which receives the lower end of that rib, the two in contact. This groove is the mating channel 56.

At the lower left corner of the sectioned spacer frame 42, a small block lies between the underside of that frame and the upwardly facing top surface of the ledge 18, contacting both and flattened between them. This block is one of the resilient feet 58.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
14, 18, 42, 56, 58, 62, 64

## Numeral targets
- 14: well inside the hatching of the upright wall body, below the closure slab.
- 18: well inside the hatching of the block projecting from the inner surface of the upright wall body.
- 42: well inside the hatching of the sectioned frame body, to the right of the groove and below it.
- 56: inside the groove in the upper edge of the sectioned frame body.
- 58: well inside the block resting on the upwardly facing top surface of the ledge.
- 62: well inside the narrow downward projection of the closure slab, above the groove it enters.
- 64: well inside the compressible body flattened between the closure slab and the top end of the upright wall body.

# FIG. 4

## View
Enlarged fragmentary vertical sectional view of a lower side region of the carrier, seen horizontally, from the lower end of a guide duct down to the condensate channel. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area, running from the upper part of the fragment down to a thick hatched horizontal bottom body that occupies the lower part of the drawing area and extends rightward.

Spaced to the right of the inner surface of the upright wall body, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, running downward and ending above the horizontal bottom body. This thin wall is one of the tray side walls 26. The open vertical space between the inner surface of the thick wall body and the left surface of the thin wall is one of the side supply passages 28, running down to the horizontal bottom body.

In the lower portion of the thin wall, a vertical series of small openings passes through it from its left surface to its right surface. These are the perforations 30.

At the top of the drawing area, above the open vertical space, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section, representing the lower outboard region of the thermal module. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50. At the lower end of the channel an opening passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface of the fragment, so the channel opens downward toward the open vertical space below. This opening is one of the discharge openings 76.

In the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body, at the foot of the open vertical space and directly below it, a shallow upwardly open trough is drawn in section, wider than it is deep. This trough is the condensate channel 70.

An elongated body of absorbent material lies in the trough, filling its lower part and following its open profile. This body is the absorbent wick 72. A narrow strip extends upward from its upper surface into the open vertical space, its free upper end clear of the surrounding surfaces. This strip is the pull tab 74.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
26, 28, 30, 50, 70, 72, 74, 76

## Numeral targets
- 26: well inside the hatching of the thin upright wall, above the small openings.
- 28: inside the open vertical space, at a height between the small openings and the top of the fragment.
- 30: on one of the small openings toward the middle of the series.
- 50: inside the open vertical channel in the body fragment at the top of the drawing area.
- 70: inside the trough at its left end, in the open space above the absorbent body.
- 72: well inside the elongated absorbent body lying in the trough.
- 74: well inside the narrow strip rising from the absorbent body, near its free upper end.
- 76: on the opening through the downwardly facing bottom surface of the body fragment.

A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area, running from the upper part of the fragment down to a thick hatched horizontal bottom body that occupies the lower part of the drawing area and extends rightward.

# FIG. 1

## View
Vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, seen horizontally. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
An upright rectangular container occupies the centre of the drawing area: a thick hatched left wall body and a thick hatched right wall body of equal height, joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body spanning between them. These form the sectioned outer shell 10, whose bottom body is the floor 12. The container is open at the top.

A thick hatched horizontal slab lies across the top ends of both wall bodies, spanning the full outer width, its underside contacting both. This slab is the insulated lid 60, closed.

Inside the container, in its lower two thirds, a sectioned open-top box is drawn with thin hatched walls: an upright left wall, an upright right wall and a horizontal bottom wall joining them. This box is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the top surface of the floor 12, and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the inner surfaces of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side running from the top of the box down to the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks stand between the underside of the tray bottom wall and the top surface of the floor 12, one near each end of the tray. These blocks are the tray feet 22. The open horizontal space between that underside and that top surface, extending between and beyond the blocks, is the lower return passage 24.

In the upper interior, between the inner surfaces of the two wall bodies and between the open top of the product tray 20 and the underside of the insulated lid 60, a horizontally elongated hatched body is drawn in section. This body is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks are drawn within it, shown schematically, spaced from one another and from its outboard ends. The hatched body is open downward at its centre between those blocks, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening downward at the lower outboard end of the body above the vertical gap beside the product tray 20.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

- 10: well inside the hatching of the left wall body.
- 12: well inside the hatching of the horizontal bottom body.

- 22: well inside the left short block standing on the floor.
- 24: inside the open horizontal space between the tray bottom wall and the floor.

# FIG. 1

## View
Vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, seen horizontally. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
An upright rectangular container occupies the centre of the drawing area: a thick hatched left wall body and a thick hatched right wall body of equal height, joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body. These form the sectioned outer shell 10, whose bottom body is the floor 12. The container is open at the top.

A thick hatched horizontal slab lies across the top ends of both wall bodies, spanning the full outer width, its underside contacting both. This slab is the insulated lid 60, closed.

Inside the container, in its lower two thirds, a sectioned open-top box is drawn with thin hatched walls: an upright left wall, an upright right wall and a horizontal bottom wall joining them. This box is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the top surface of the floor 12, and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the inner surfaces of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side running from the top of the box down to the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks stand between the underside of the tray bottom wall and the top surface of the floor 12, one near each end of the tray. These blocks are the tray feet 22. The open horizontal space between that underside and that top surface, extending between and beyond the blocks, is the lower return passage 24.

In the upper interior, between the inner surfaces of the two wall bodies and between the open top of the product tray 20 and the underside of the insulated lid 60, a horizontally elongated hatched body is drawn in section. This body is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks are drawn within it, shown schematically, spaced from one another and from its outboard ends. The hatched body is open downward at its centre between those blocks, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening downward at the lower outboard end of the body above the vertical gap beside the product tray 20.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

## Numeral targets
- 10: well inside the hatching of the left wall body.
- 12: well inside the hatching of the horizontal bottom body.

- 22: well inside the left short block standing on the floor.

- 40: well inside the hatching of the elongated upper body, between its centre and its left end, clear of the upright blocks.

# FIG. 2

## View
Perspective view of the thermal module alone, removed from the carrier, seen from above and in front so that the open top, the near long side and the near short end are visible. Plain black line work on white, no hatching. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
The main body is an upright rectangular open frame, longer from left to right than it is deep from front to back, and lower in height than it is deep. It has a near long side wall, a far long side wall, a left short end wall, a right short end wall and a bottom panel joining them. The top is open. This frame is the spacer frame 42; the frame with the slabs below is the thermal module 40.

Two flat rectangular slabs stand upright inside the frame, each parallel to the long side walls and running most of the frame length. They are spaced apart across the depth of the frame, leaving an open central gap between their confronting broad faces, and each is also spaced from the adjacent long side wall, leaving an open vertical channel between slab and wall. The slab nearer the front is the first phase-change cassette 44; the slab nearer the back is the second phase-change cassette 46. Each slab is a plain closed rectangular box, shown schematically, its upper edge below the top edges of the frame walls.

In the bottom panel, within the open central gap between the slabs, a rectangular through opening is drawn, so the viewer looks down through the panel there. This opening is the central inlet opening 48.

Along the lower part of the near long side wall, at the foot of the channel between the first phase-change cassette 44 and that wall, a horizontal row of rectangular openings passes through the wall. These are the peripheral outlet openings 54. A matching row is drawn along the lower part of the far long side wall where visible.

The top edge of the left short end wall carries an upwardly open groove running across the full depth of that wall from front to back and interrupting the top edge. This groove is the mating channel 56.

Four small blocks project downward from the underside of the bottom panel at its corners, two visible at the front. These blocks are the resilient feet 58.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 54, 56, 58

## Numeral targets
- 40: on the outer surface of the near long side wall, above the row of openings and toward the right end.
- 42: on the outer surface of the right short end wall, well inside its outline.
- 44: well inside the visible upper face of the front slab.
- 46: well inside the visible upper face of the rear slab.
- 48: well inside the rectangular through opening in the bottom panel.
- 54: on one opening toward the middle of the row in the near long side wall.
- 56: well inside the groove in the top edge of the left short end wall.
- 58: well inside one of the small blocks below the front corners of the bottom panel.

# FIG. 5

## View
Enlarged fragmentary sectional view through a wall of the outer shell at the mechanical exposure indicator, seen horizontally, with the indicator stem in the exposed position. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
A thick hatched upright wall body stands across the middle of the drawing area, its outer surface facing left and its inner surface facing right. This wall body is the sectioned outer shell 10. A horizontal bore passes through it from outer to inner surface at mid height.

A tubular body is seated in the bore and shown in section, its cut walls appearing as a hatched upper wall and a hatched lower wall with an open bore between them, the tubular body spanning the full thickness of the wall body and open at both ends. This tubular body is the body of the mechanical exposure indicator 80. Its bore is wider at the part nearer the inner surface than at the part nearer the outer surface, the step between the two widths forming an internal shoulder facing left.

An elongated horizontal shaft lies in the bore and extends beyond both ends of the tubular body: to the left it projects past the outer surface of the wall body into the open space at the left of the drawing area, and to the right its inner end reaches into the open space at the right. This shaft is the indicator stem 82. A collar is drawn on the shaft within the wider part of the bore, standing proud of the shaft all round.

A coil spring surrounds the shaft in the wider part of the bore, drawn as a series of aligned loops between the internal shoulder and the left face of the collar and shown compressed between them. This spring is the spring 86.

A small block sits in a recess in the hatched upper wall of the tubular body, above the shaft and to the right of the collar, projecting downward from the recess with its lower end adjacent the upper surface of the shaft. This block is the temperature-responsive latch 84.

In the open space at the right of the drawing area, spaced from the inner surface of the wall body, an upright plain rectangular block is drawn, shown schematically, its left face confronting and contacting the inner end of the shaft. This block is the first phase-change cassette 44.

# FIG. 1

## View
Vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, seen horizontally. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
An upright rectangular container occupies the centre of the drawing area: a thick hatched left wall body and a thick hatched right wall body of equal height, joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body. These form the sectioned outer shell 10, whose bottom body is the floor 12. The container is open at the top.

A thick hatched horizontal slab lies across the top ends of both wall bodies, spanning the full outer width, its underside contacting both. This slab is the insulated lid 60, closed.

Inside the container, in its lower two thirds, a sectioned open-top box is drawn with thin hatched walls: an upright left wall, an upright right wall and a horizontal bottom wall joining them. This box is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the top surface of the floor 12, and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the inner surfaces of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side running from the top of the box down to the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks stand between the underside of the tray bottom wall and the top surface of the floor 12, one near each end of the tray. These blocks are the tray feet 22. The open horizontal space between that underside and that top surface, extending between and beyond the blocks, is the lower return passage 24.

In the upper interior, between the inner surfaces of the two wall bodies and between the open top of the product tray 20 and the underside of the insulated lid 60, a horizontally elongated hatched body is drawn in section. This body is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks are drawn within it, shown schematically, spaced from one another and from its outboard ends. The hatched body is open downward at its centre between those blocks, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening downward above the vertical gap beside the product tray 20.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

## Numeral targets

- 12: well inside the hatching of the horizontal bottom body.

# FIG. 2

## View
Perspective view of the thermal module alone, seen from above and in front so that the open top, the near long side and the near short end are visible. Plain black line work on white, no hatching. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
The main body is an upright rectangular open frame, longer from left to right than it is deep from front to back, and lower in height than it is deep. It has a near long side wall, a far long side wall, a left short end wall, a right short end wall and a bottom panel joining them. The top is open. This frame is the spacer frame 42; the frame with the slabs below is the thermal module 40.

Two flat rectangular slabs stand upright inside the frame, each parallel to the long side walls and running most of the frame length. They are spaced apart across the depth of the frame, leaving an open central gap between their confronting broad faces, and each is also spaced from the adjacent long side wall, leaving an open vertical channel between slab and wall. The slab nearer the front is the first phase-change cassette 44; the slab nearer the back is the second phase-change cassette 46. Each slab is a plain closed box, shown schematically, its upper edge below the top edges of the frame walls.

In the bottom panel, within the open central gap between the slabs, a rectangular through opening is drawn, so the viewer looks down through the panel there. This opening is the central inlet opening 48.

Along the lower part of the near long side wall, at the foot of the channel between the first phase-change cassette 44 and that wall, a horizontal row of rectangular openings passes through the wall. These are the peripheral outlet openings 54. A matching row is drawn along the far long side wall where visible.

The top edge of the left short end wall carries an upwardly open groove running across the full depth of that wall from front to back. This groove is the mating channel 56.

Four small blocks project downward from the underside of the bottom panel at its corners, two visible at the front. These blocks are the resilient feet 58.

A passive cold-chain carrier is disclosed in which the closing of the lid, rather than the care of the packer, establishes the circulation path.

In one aspect, the carrier includes an insulated outer shell having a floor and side walls, a product tray removably received in the outer shell, a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, and an insulated lid. The product tray is supported above the floor by tray feet so that a lower return passage remains between the product tray and the floor, and the tray side walls are spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell to form two side supply passages. The thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings. The insulated lid carries a depending indexing rib positioned to enter a mating channel of the spacer frame as the lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.

In the registered position the shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the lid cooperate to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the circulation is driven by the density difference between the air warmed in the product region and the air cooled along the cassette faces.

The technical effect of lid-driven registration is that the alignment on which the circulation path depends is created by an act the packer cannot omit. The thermal module may be dropped into the shell approximately, offset or skewed, and the descending indexing rib entering the mating channel translates the module into the position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The seal made by a compressible lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell occurs after registration, so the carrier is not closed against a module that is still out of position. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, so that the registered module is held down against the product tray and cannot lift away from it under the vibration and inversion of transport.

In a further aspect, a shallow condensate channel extends around the product tray and receives a removable absorbent wick. Discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts deliver condensate that forms on the cassettes into the condensate channel. A pull tab on the absorbent wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, so the wick is replaced without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service.

In a further aspect, the outer shell carries a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside the carrier. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position, and the indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again, being reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator therefore reports the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends, survives recovery of the cassette, and requires no battery. The exposure indicator does not control airflow, so the circulation path is unaffected by whether the indicator has tripped.

In a further aspect, a method includes fitting conditioned phase-change cassettes to the spacer frame, placing product in the product tray, placing the product tray in the outer shell, placing the thermal module above the product tray, and closing the insulated lid so that the depending indexing rib enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into the registered position, whereafter air circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover.

The features summarised above may be used together or separately, and the summary is not a statement of the scope of the claims.

content.text:
The draft is complete: all ten body sections, the numeral table, and five figure specifications.

**What is in claim 1**, and why: the registered passive circulation path plus lid-driven registration, which the disclosure names as the essential relationship. Concretely, claim 1 ties four cooperating bodies (shell, suspended perforated tray, spacer-frame module with central inlet, opposed cassettes, outboard guide ducts and peripheral outlets, and a lid whose depending indexing rib enters the frame's mating channel) into one closed loop: rise at the centre, split along the cassette faces, descend outboard, cross the tray perforations, return beneath the tray. The rib-and-channel registration does real work: it is the only element that makes the outlet-to-passage overlap independent of how the packer set the module down, and the specification states that problem and that effect before it is needed in argument.

**Deliberately left out of claim 1:** the gasket, the ledge-and-resilient-foot retention, the condensate channel, the wick and pull tab, and the exposure indicator. Each is disclosed as optional or as a consequence of closing, so each became a dependent claim (3, 2, 8 to 10, 11 to 14) rather than scope surrendered up front. I kept the negative recitation that the carrier is free of a fan, pump or powered air mover, because the inventor states passivity as the character of the invention and it separates the loop from forced-air shippers.

**Three statutory hooks:** the carrier (claim 1), the thermal module alone (claim 16, infringed by a module or cassette-kit supplier), and the method of transporting (claim 20, infringed by the packer and shipper).

**Two places I wrote supported functional language instead of inventing detail:** the shape of the rib-and-channel engagement is described only as shaped so that engagement during closing travel translates the frame horizontally (I removed an earlier tapered-surface claim rather than claim geometry the disclosure does not supply), and the exposed position of the indicator stem is described as projecting beyond, or presenting a contrasting portion at, the outer surface.

**On prior art:** `prior_art/INDEX.md` lists no references, so the Background contains no citations, and no reference-clearing argument could be built against actual documents. As the brief anticipates, the art you were given may be incomplete, and the Background is written from the general problem rather than from any document.

input.summary: Wrote the complete first draft of the application for the passive cold-chain carrier: all ten body sections in draft/, the reference-numeral table, and five figure specifications (whole-carrier section, thermal module perspective, lid-registration detail, condensate detail, exposure-indicator detail). Claim 1 recites the lid-registered passive circulation path around the suspended perforated tray and opposed cassettes; independent claims also cover the thermal module alone and the method of transporting. prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and the art available to this draft may be incomplete.
reasoning: Claim 1 was built around the one relationship the disclosure calls essential: the registered circulation path (centre rise, split along opposed cassette faces, descend outboard guide ducts, cross the side supply passages and tray perforations, return beneath the tray) combined with a lid-carried depending indexing rib that enters a mating channel of the spacer frame and shifts the module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. Registration does technical work rather than being decorative: it is what makes the flow geometry independent of how the packer set the module down, and the Background and Detailed Description state that problem and that effect expressly so a later argument has something in the specification to stand on.

The negative recitation that the carrier is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover stayed in claim 1. In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 need only be dropped into the outer shell 10 approximately, and may be set down offset or skewed within the clearance available to it. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is then created by closing the lid, which is an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 project inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10 beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the confronting inner faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces. Each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: the cooled air is produced at the top of the carrier and is given a continuous downward path of its own along the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, while the warmed air is given a continuous upward path through the product region to the central inlet opening 48, and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 6, the outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 need only be dropped into the outer shell 10 approximately, and may be set down offset or skewed within the clearance available to it. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is then created by closing the lid, which is an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 project inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10 beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the confronting inner faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces. Each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: the cooled air is produced at the top of the carrier and is given a continuous downward path of its own along the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, while the warmed air is given a continuous upward path through the product region to the central inlet opening 48, and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream.

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 6, the outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, phase-change cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by the payload are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Alternatives

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

# FIG. 1

## View
Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, seen horizontally. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
An upright rectangular container occupies the centre of the drawing area: a thick hatched left wall body and a thick hatched right wall body of equal height, joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body. These form the sectioned outer shell 10, whose bottom body is the floor 12. The container is open at the top.

A thick hatched horizontal slab lies across the top ends of both wall bodies, spanning the full outer width, its underside overlying the top ends of both wall bodies. This slab is the insulated lid 60, closed. The gasket interface at those top ends is shown enlarged in FIG. 3.

Inside the container, in its lower two thirds, a sectioned open-top box is drawn with thin hatched walls: an upright left wall, an upright right wall and a horizontal bottom wall joining them. This box is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the top surface of the floor 12, and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the inner surfaces of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side running from the top of the box down to the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks stand between the underside of the tray bottom wall and the top surface of the floor 12, one near each end of the tray. These blocks are the tray feet 22. The open horizontal space between that underside and that top surface, extending between and beyond the blocks, is the lower return passage 24.

In the upper interior, between the inner surfaces of the two wall bodies and between the open top of the product tray 20 and the underside of the insulated lid 60, a horizontally elongated hatched body is drawn in section. This body is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks are drawn within it, shown schematically, spaced from one another and from its outboard ends. The hatched body is open downward at its centre between those blocks, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the vertical gap beside the product tray 20.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

## Numeral targets
- 10: well inside the hatching of the left wall body.
- 12: well inside the hatching of the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left upright wall of the open-top box.
- 22: well inside the left short block on the floor.
- 24: inside the open space between the tray bottom wall and the floor.
- 40: well inside the elongated upper body, clear of the upright blocks.
- 60: well inside the horizontal slab at the top.
- 100: outside the container, clear of all line work, with a lead line ending in an arrow directed at the assembled carrier as a whole.

## View
Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, seen horizontally. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
An upright rectangular container occupies the centre of the drawing area: a thick hatched left wall body and a thick hatched right wall body of equal height, joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body. These form the sectioned outer shell 10, whose bottom body is the floor 12. The container is open at the top.

A thick hatched horizontal slab lies across the top ends of both wall bodies, spanning the full outer width, its underside overlying the top ends of both wall bodies. This slab is the insulated lid 60, closed. The gasket interface at those top ends is shown enlarged in FIG. 3.

Inside the container, in its lower two thirds, a sectioned open-top box is drawn with thin hatched walls: an upright left wall, an upright right wall and a horizontal bottom wall joining them. This box is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the top surface of the floor 12, and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the inner surfaces of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side running from the top of the box down to the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks stand between the underside of the tray bottom wall and the top surface of the floor 12, one near each end of the tray. These blocks are the tray feet 22. The open horizontal space between that underside and that top surface, extending between and beyond the blocks, is the lower return passage 24.

In the upper interior, between the inner surfaces of the two wall bodies and between the open top of the product tray 20 and the underside of the insulated lid 60, a horizontally elongated hatched body is drawn in section. This body is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks are drawn within it, shown schematically, spaced from one another and from its outboard ends. The hatched body is open downward at its centre between those blocks, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the vertical gap beside the product tray 20.

10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100
