A passive cold-chain carrier is disclosed in which the closing of the lid, rather than the care of the packer, establishes the circulation path.

In one aspect, the carrier includes an insulated outer shell having a floor and side walls, a product tray removably received in the outer shell, a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, and an insulated lid. The product tray is supported above the floor by tray feet so that a lower return passage remains between the product tray and the floor, and the tray side walls are spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell to form two side supply passages. The thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings. The insulated lid carries a depending indexing rib positioned to enter a mating channel of the spacer frame as the lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.

In the registered position the shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the lid cooperate to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the circulation is driven by the density difference between the air warmed in the product region and the air cooled along the cassette faces.

The technical effect of lid-driven registration is that the alignment on which the circulation path depends is created by an act the packer cannot omit. The thermal module may be dropped into the outer shell approximately, offset or skewed, and the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel translates the module into the position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The seal made by a compressible lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell occurs after registration, so the carrier is not closed against a module that is still out of position. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, so that the registered module is held down against the product tray and cannot lift away from it under the vibration and inversion of transport.

In a further aspect, a shallow condensate channel extends around the product tray and receives a removable absorbent wick. Discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts deliver condensate that forms on the cassettes into the condensate channel. A pull tab on the absorbent wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, so the wick is replaced without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service.

In a further aspect, the outer shell carries a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside the carrier. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position, and the indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again, being reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator therefore reports the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends, survives recovery of the cassette, and requires no battery. The exposure indicator does not control airflow, so the circulation path is unaffected by whether the indicator has tripped.

In a further aspect, a method includes fitting conditioned phase-change cassettes to the spacer frame, placing product in the product tray, placing the product tray in the outer shell, placing the thermal module above the product tray, and closing the insulated lid so that the depending indexing rib enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into the registered position, whereafter air circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover.

The features summarised above may be used together or separately, and the summary is not a statement of the scope of the claims.

5:Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.
9:The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.
13:Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.
15:The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.
21:The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.
25:The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 project inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10 beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.
35:A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.
41:The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.

All findings are addressed. Summary of what changed:

**Untraced technical matter removed.** All material and construction menus are gone (shell and lid now read "formed of thermally insulating material"; the tray-foot, resilient-foot and wick alternative sentences are deleted). Cassette construction is now "Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material." The "holds the cassettes clear of the product tray" sentence and its no-contact effect are deleted, and claim 6 is reduced to removability of the cassettes. Perforation wall, hole shape and lengthwise distribution are deleted and the claim reciting them is cancelled. The indicator's bore, stepped shoulder, collar and latch recess are gone from both the description and the drawing brief, leaving stem, latch and spring with the indicator body shown schematically. "Conductive contact" is back to "thermally coupled" in the description and the figure, and that claim is cancelled. 1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	Source ledger traced across draft/01–10, numerals.md and figures/fig-01…06.md against input/disclosure.md and the single USER passage in input/conversation.md (which is verbatim identical to the disclosure). input/brief.md was used only for title, applicant/inventor, no-priority and no-government-support, all of which match draft/01, 02 and 03. The abstract is 141 words and single-paragraph. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions or unresolved alternatives remain in any file. Numerals.md defines 31 numerals, each used in the description with one meaning, and no numeral appears in a figure brief without a definition.
4	
5	Most of the skeleton traces cleanly: shell/floor/side walls, tray on feet with lower return passage, tray side walls spaced inward forming two side supply passages, perforations, rigid spacer frame with two opposed cassettes, central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with (overlapping) the side supply passages, the full circulation path, absence of fan/pump/powered air mover, depending indexing rib entering a mating channel to shift the module into the registered position, gasket sealing after registration, resilient feet pressed against shell ledges, condensate channel with removable wick and pull tab, guide-duct openings discharging condensate, and the whole exposure-indicator chain (stem thermally coupled to one cassette, temperature-responsive latch, spring, latched exposed position, manual reset after opening, no airflow control). The method claims 18–21 track the disclosure's "For use" paragraph. Background prior-art characterisations are not charged against the inventor sources per instruction.
6	
7	Fourteen items do not trace, or are internally inconsistent, and are reported below. The most serious is structural: the draft invents a second, distinct set of openings. The disclosure states only "Openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel," yet the draft places peripheral outlet openings 54 at the lower ends of the guide ducts and then asserts discharge openings 76 that are "separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54" - in the Summary, the description, dependent claims 8 and 17, and FIG. 5. Nothing in the sources affirms two separate sets; that separateness is a new limitation and is reported critical.
8	
9	Three further disclosure-fidelity gaps are reported major: (a) the convection mechanism and flow-topology reasoning added at Summary ¶5 and description ¶31 ("Circulation is driven by the density difference…", "the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20", "the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream"), for which the only source wording is "Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet"; (b) the inner-face/outer-face crossover topology ("two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces", "each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face", claim 5, and FIG. 2's cassette upper edges drawn below the frame top edges so air crosses over the cassettes), where the source says only "divides along faces of the cassettes" and "two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes"; and (c) the dependent-claim 7 positional limitation "at a lower region of the outer shell beneath the side supply passages", where the source says only "a shallow condensate channel around the product tray".
10	
11	Four verified internal inconsistencies are reported major. First, the mating channel 56 is placed in FIG. 2 on "the top edge of the left short end wall" but FIG. 3 - an enlargement of an upper side region of FIG. 1, in the same fragment as ledge 18 and resilient foot 58, which FIG. 2 puts on the long side - shows the groove there; one section plane cannot contain both. Second, FIG. 1's Geometry-to-draw omits every feature its own enlargements are said to enlarge: no indexing rib 62, gasket 64, ledge 18, perforations 30, condensate channel 70 or wick 72 appear in the parent view, so FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 enlarge regions that do not contain the detail. Third, FIG. 6 draws the coil spring 86 "shown compressed" while the stem stands in the exposed position, contradicting description ¶41 and claim 10, in which the spring biases the stem toward the exposed position and moves it there on release. Fourth, FIG. 4 draws perforations 30 passing through the tray side wall "from its left surface to its right surface", i.e. into the tray interior, while description ¶9 says they "open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24"; FIG. 4 shows no tray bottom wall, so as briefed the flow path contradicts both the description and the disclosed order "enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage".
12	
13	Six minor items are reported: the gasket's unsourced "extends around an underside … outboard of the depending indexing rib" (claim 4, ¶21); the unsourced siting of ledges as inward projections of the side walls and feet at "lower outboard regions" (claims 2, 15, 16, ¶17, ¶25); two unsourced indicator qualifiers ("when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position"; "the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition") together with FIG. 6 drawing the stem's inner end spaced across a gap from cassette 44 despite the recited thermal coupling; the Brief Description's narrowing of the perforations to "a tray side wall" against the description's "through the product tray 20"; the unsourced skew-correction capability ("offset or skewed", Summary ¶7 and ¶23); and two FIG. 2 briefing defects - numeral 40 targeted onto the spacer frame's own wall where it cannot be distinguished from 42, and an unsourced count of "a horizontal row of rectangular openings" per guide duct.

# FIG. 2

## View
Perspective view of the thermal module alone, seen from above and in front so that the open top, the near long side and the near short end are visible. Plain black line work on white, no hatching. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
The main body is a rectangular open frame, shown schematically. It has a near long side wall, a far long side wall, a left short end wall, a right short end wall and a bottom panel joining them. The top is open. This frame is the spacer frame 42; the spacer frame 42 together with the two slabs it holds is the thermal module 40.

Two flat rectangular slabs stand upright inside the frame, each parallel to the long side walls and running most of the frame length. They are spaced apart across the depth of the frame, leaving an open central gap between their confronting broad faces, and each is also spaced from the adjacent long side wall, leaving an open vertical channel between slab and wall. The slab nearer the front is the first phase-change cassette 44; the slab nearer the back is the second phase-change cassette 46. Each slab is a plain closed box, shown schematically.

In the bottom panel, within the open central gap between the slabs, a rectangular through opening is drawn, so the viewer looks down through the panel there. This opening is the central inlet opening 48.

Along the lower part of the near long side wall, at the foot of the channel between the first phase-change cassette 44 and that wall, a single rectangular opening passes through the wall. This is one of the peripheral outlet openings 54. A matching opening is drawn in the far long side wall where visible.

The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove at mid-length, running across the thickness of that wall. This groove is the mating channel 56.

Small blocks project downward from the underside of the frame, two visible at the front, shown schematically. These blocks are the resilient feet 58.

40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 54, 56, 58

lines: Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

-The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

+The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 need only be dropped into the outer shell 10 approximately, and may be set down offset or skewed within the clearance available to it. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is then created by closing the lid, which is an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

lines: The circulation path

-In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the confronting inner faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces. Each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

+In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: the cooled air is produced at the top of the carrier and is given a continuous downward path of its own along the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, while the warmed air is given a continuous upward path through the product region to the central inlet opening 48, and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream.

-The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. +The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

A passive cold-chain carrier is disclosed in which the closing of the lid, rather than the care of the packer, establishes the circulation path.

In one aspect, the carrier includes an insulated outer shell having a floor and side walls, a product tray removably received in the outer shell, a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, and an insulated lid. The product tray is supported above the floor by tray feet so that a lower return passage remains between the product tray and the floor, and the tray side walls are spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell to form two side supply passages. The thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings. The insulated lid carries a depending indexing rib positioned to enter a mating channel of the spacer frame as the lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.

In the registered position the shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the lid cooperate to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the circulation is driven by the density difference between the air warmed in the product region and the air cooled along the cassette faces.

The technical effect of lid-driven registration is that the alignment on which the circulation path depends is created by an act the packer cannot omit. The thermal module may be dropped into the outer shell approximately, offset or skewed, and the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel translates the module into the position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The seal made by a compressible lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell occurs after registration, so the carrier is not closed against a module that is still out of position. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, so that the registered module is held down against the product tray and cannot lift away from it under the vibration and inversion of transport.

In a further aspect, a shallow condensate channel extends around the product tray and receives a removable absorbent wick. Discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, separate from the peripheral outlet openings, deliver condensate into the condensate channel. A pull tab on the absorbent wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, so the wick is replaced without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service.

In a further aspect, the outer shell carries a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside the carrier. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position, and the indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again, being reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator therefore reports the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends, survives recovery of the cassette, and requires no battery. The exposure indicator does not control airflow, so the circulation path is unaffected by whether the indicator has tripped.

In a further aspect, a method includes fitting conditioned phase-change cassettes to the spacer frame, placing product in the product tray, placing the product tray in the outer shell, placing the thermal module above the product tray, and closing the insulated lid so that the depending indexing rib enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into the registered position, whereafter air circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover.

The features summarised above may be used together or separately, and the summary is not a statement of the scope of the claims.

1. A passive cold-chain carrier comprising:

an insulated outer shell having a floor, side walls and an upper edge;

a product tray removably received in the outer shell, the product tray having a bottom wall, tray side walls, perforations, and tray feet standing on the floor so that the product tray is supported above the floor and a lower return passage remains between the bottom wall and the floor, the tray side walls being spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell so that two side supply passages are formed;

a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, the thermal module comprising a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, and a mating channel; and

an insulated lid closable on the upper edge of the outer shell and carrying a depending indexing rib positioned to enter the mating channel as the insulated lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages;

the carrier being free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the outer shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the insulated lid cooperating in the registered position to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through the perforations, and returns through the lower return passage.

2. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the spacer frame carries resilient feet, the outer shell has ledges beneath the resilient feet, and closure of the insulated lid presses the resilient feet against the ledges so that the thermal module is held down against lifting away from the product tray.

3. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a compressible lid gasket carried by the insulated lid and arranged to seal against the upper edge of the outer shell after the depending indexing rib has shifted the thermal module into the registered position.

4. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the two opposed phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame with an inner face of a first phase-change cassette confronting an inner face of a second phase-change cassette across a central space, and the central inlet opening opens downward into the central space.

5. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame.

6. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a shallow condensate channel extending around the product tray, and a removable absorbent wick lying in the condensate channel.

7. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 6, wherein openings at lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the condensate channel.

8. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 6, wherein the absorbent wick carries a pull tab that remains accessible when the product tray is removed from the outer shell, so that the absorbent wick is replaceable without opening a phase-change cassette.

9. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a mechanical exposure indicator carried by the outer shell and visible from outside the carrier, the mechanical exposure indicator comprising an indicator stem thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes, a temperature-responsive latch retaining the indicator stem in a stowed position, and a spring biasing the indicator stem toward an exposed position, the temperature-responsive latch releasing the indicator stem when said one of the phase-change cassettes softens.

10. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 9, wherein the exposed position is a latched position in which the mechanical exposure indicator retains the indicator stem after said one of the phase-change cassettes has cooled again, the mechanical exposure indicator being resettable manually only after the carrier is opened.

11. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 9, wherein the mechanical exposure indicator does not control airflow, the circulation path being the same whether or not the indicator stem stands in the exposed position.

12. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the depending indexing rib meets the mating channel while the insulated lid is spaced above the upper edge of the outer shell, and remaining closing travel of the insulated lid translates the spacer frame horizontally into the registered position.

13. A thermal module for a passive cold-chain carrier having an insulated outer shell, a product tray defining side supply passages with side walls of the outer shell, and an insulated lid carrying a depending indexing rib, the thermal module comprising:

a rigid spacer frame sized to be removably received in the outer shell above the product tray; and

two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame;

the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening through which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the spacer frame, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes and receiving air that has divided along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, and a mating channel positioned to be entered by the depending indexing rib as the insulated lid closes so that the thermal module is shifted into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.

14. The thermal module of claim 13, further comprising resilient feet carried by the spacer frame, the resilient feet being positioned to be pressed against ledges of the outer shell by closure of the insulated lid so that the thermal module is held down against the product tray.

15. The thermal module of claim 13, wherein the mating channel opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame.

16. The thermal module of claim 13, wherein openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts are positioned to discharge condensate into a condensate channel of the outer shell.

17. A method of transporting temperature-sensitive goods, the method comprising:

fitting two conditioned phase-change cassettes to a rigid spacer frame of a thermal module, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, and a mating channel;

placing the goods in a product tray and placing the product tray in an insulated outer shell so that tray feet of the product tray stand on a floor of the outer shell, leaving a lower return passage between the product tray and the floor and two side supply passages between tray side walls of the product tray and side walls of the outer shell;

placing the thermal module in the outer shell above the product tray;

closing an insulated lid on an upper edge of the outer shell so that a depending indexing rib carried by the insulated lid enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages; and

thereafter transporting the goods while air circulates, without operation of any powered air mover, along a circulation path in which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage.

18. The method of claim 17, wherein closing the insulated lid further presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, retaining the thermal module against lifting away from the product tray during the transporting, and compresses a compressible lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell after the thermal module has been shifted into the registered position.

19. The method of claim 17, further comprising, after the transporting, opening the insulated lid, removing the product tray from the outer shell, and drawing a removable absorbent wick out of a condensate channel of the outer shell by a pull tab of the absorbent wick without opening a phase-change cassette.

20. The method of claim 17, further comprising reading, from outside the outer shell, a mechanical exposure indicator having an indicator stem thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes, the indicator stem having been moved by a spring to a latched exposed position on release of a temperature-responsive latch by softening of said one of the phase-change cassettes and remaining in the latched exposed position after said one of the phase-change cassettes has cooled again, and resetting the mechanical exposure indicator manually after the insulated lid has been opened.

# FIG. 1

## View
Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry to draw
Two thick hatched upright wall bodies, joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body, form an upright container at the centre of the drawing area, open at the top. These are the sectioned outer shell 10, whose bottom body is the floor 12. A block projects inward from each wall body below its top end.

A thick hatched horizontal slab lies across the top ends of both wall bodies, overlying those top ends. This slab is the insulated lid 60, closed. A narrow rib projects downward from its underside on each side, inboard of those top ends, and a small compressible body lies between the slab and each top end. That interface is enlarged in FIG. 3.

Inside the container, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched upright walls and a horizontal bottom wall is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the floor 12, and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side running down to the floor 12. Below the level of that bottom wall, small openings pass through each upright wall of the box.

Two short hatched blocks stand between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12. These blocks are the tray feet 22. The open space between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12 is the lower return passage 24. A shallow upwardly open trough is formed in the floor 12 at the foot of each vertical gap, with an elongated absorbent body lying in it.

Between the open top of the product tray 20 and the underside of the insulated lid 60, an elongated hatched body is drawn in section. This body is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks are drawn within it, shown schematically, spaced from one another and from its ends. The body is open downward at its centre, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the vertical gap.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

## Numeral targets
- 10: well inside the hatching of the left wall body.
- 12: well inside the hatching of the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left upright wall of the open-top box.
- 22: well inside the left short block on the floor.
- 24: inside the open space between the tray bottom wall and the floor.
- 40: outside the container, clear of all line work, with a lead line and arrow directed at the module as a whole.
- 60: well inside the horizontal slab at the top.
- 100: outside the container, clear of all line work, with a lead line and arrow directed at the assembled carrier as a whole.

13	Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.
14	
15	The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.
16	
17	The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.
18	
19	Registration and retention by the lid
20	
21	The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.
22	
23	This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.
24

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76 at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.

# FIG. 1

## View
Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry to draw
Two thick hatched upright wall bodies, joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body, form an upright container at the centre of the drawing area, open at the top. These are the sectioned outer shell 10, whose bottom body is the floor 12. A block projects inward from each wall body below its top end.

A thick hatched horizontal slab lies across the top ends of both wall bodies, overlying those top ends. This slab is the insulated lid 60, closed. A narrow rib projects downward from its underside, inboard of the top end of the left wall body, and a small compressible body lies between the slab and each top end. That interface is enlarged in FIG. 3.

Inside the container, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched upright walls and a horizontal bottom wall is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the floor 12, and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side running down to the floor 12. Below the level of that bottom wall, small openings pass through each upright wall of the box.

Two short hatched blocks stand between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12. These blocks are the tray feet 22. The open space between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12 is the lower return passage 24. A shallow upwardly open trough is formed in the floor 12 at the foot of each vertical gap, with an elongated absorbent body lying in it.

Between the open top of the product tray 20 and the underside of the insulated lid 60, an elongated hatched body is drawn in section. This body is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks are drawn within it, shown schematically, spaced from one another and from its ends. The body is open downward at its centre, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the vertical gap.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

## Numeral targets
- 10: well inside the hatching of the left wall body.
- 12: well inside the hatching of the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left upright wall of the open-top box.
- 22: well inside the left short block on the floor.
- 24: inside the open space between the tray bottom wall and the floor.
- 40: outside the container, clear of all line work, with a lead line and arrow directed at the module as a whole.
- 60: well inside the horizontal slab at the top.
- 100: outside the container, clear of all line work, with a lead line and arrow directed at the assembled carrier as a whole.

# FIG. 1

## View
Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material, all line work well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry to draw
Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body form an upright container at the centre of the drawing area, open at the top. These are the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body being the floor 12. A block projects inward from each wall body below its top end.

A thick hatched horizontal slab lies across the top ends of both wall bodies. This slab is the insulated lid 60, closed. A narrow rib projects downward from its underside inboard of the left wall body top end, and a small compressible body lies between the slab and each top end.

Inside the container, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched upright walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the floor 12, and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side. The lower edge of each upright wall meets the floor 12 just inboard of the trough described below, and small openings pass through each upright wall below the bottom wall level, so the gap communicates with the space beneath the bottom wall only through those openings.

Two short hatched blocks between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12 are the tray feet 22. The open space between that bottom wall and the floor 12 is the lower return passage 24. A shallow upwardly open trough in the floor 12 at the foot of each gap holds an elongated absorbent body.

Between the open top of the product tray 20 and the lid 60 underside, an elongated hatched body drawn in section is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it, spaced from one another and from its ends. The body is open downward at its centre, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the gap. An upwardly open groove in its top surface beneath the narrow rib receives the lower end of that rib.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

- 10: outside the container, clear of line work, with a lead line and arrow to the outer shell as a whole.

- 24: inside the open space beneath the tray bottom wall.

# FIG. 5

## View
Enlarged view of the condensate channel region of FIG. 1, seen horizontally in section. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area, running from the upper part of the fragment down to a thick hatched horizontal bottom body that occupies the lower part and extends rightward.

In the upper right part of the drawing area, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50. At the lower end of the channel, an opening passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface of the fragment. This opening is one of the discharge openings 76.

Below the body fragment, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, spaced to the right of the inner surface of the upright wall body and ending above the horizontal bottom body. An open vertical space runs down between the upright wall body and the thin wall, from beneath the body fragment to the horizontal bottom body, so that the downward opening in the fragment stands above that space.

In the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body, at the foot of the open vertical space and below the discharge opening 76, a shallow upwardly open trough is drawn in section, wider than it is deep. This trough is the condensate channel 70.

An elongated body of absorbent material lies in the trough, filling its lower part, shown schematically. This body is the absorbent wick 72. A narrow strip extends upward from its upper surface into the open vertical space, its free upper end clear of the surrounding surfaces. This strip is the pull tab 74.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
50, 70, 72, 74, 76

## Numeral targets
- 50: inside the open vertical channel in the body fragment.
- 70: inside the trough at its left end, above the absorbent body.
- 72: well inside the elongated absorbent body lying in the trough.
- 74: well inside the narrow strip rising from the absorbent body.
- 76: on the opening through the bottom surface of the body fragment.

# FIG. 2

## View
Perspective view of the thermal module alone, seen from above and in front so that the open top, the near long side and the near short end are visible. Plain black line work on white, no hatching. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
The main body is a rectangular open frame, shown schematically. It has a near long side wall, a far long side wall, a left short end wall, a right short end wall and a bottom panel joining them. The top is open. This frame is the spacer frame 42; the spacer frame 42 together with the two slabs it holds is the thermal module 40.

Two flat rectangular slabs stand upright inside the frame, each parallel to the long side walls and running most of the frame length. They are spaced apart across the depth of the frame, leaving an open central gap between their confronting broad faces, and each is also spaced from the adjacent long side wall, leaving an open vertical channel between slab and wall. The slab nearer the front is the first phase-change cassette 44; the slab nearer the back is the second phase-change cassette 46. Each slab is a plain closed box, shown schematically.

In the bottom panel, within the open central gap between the slabs, a rectangular through opening is drawn, so the viewer looks down through the panel there. This opening is the central inlet opening 48.

Along the lower part of the near long side wall, at the foot of the channel between the first phase-change cassette 44 and that wall, a single rectangular opening passes through the wall. This is one of the peripheral outlet openings 54. A matching opening is drawn in the far long side wall where visible.

The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove at mid-length, running across the thickness of that wall. This groove is the mating channel 56.

Small blocks project downward from the underside of the frame, two visible at the front, shown schematically. These blocks are the resilient feet 58.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 54, 56, 58

## Numeral targets
- 40: outside the frame outline, clear of all line work, with a lead line and arrow directed at the module as a whole.
- 42: on the right short end wall, well inside its outline.
- 44: well inside the visible upper face of the front slab.
- 46: well inside the visible upper face of the rear slab.
- 48: well inside the through opening in the bottom panel.
- 54: on the opening in the near long side wall.
- 56: well inside the groove in the top edge of the near long side wall.
- 58: well inside one of the small blocks projecting below the frame at the front.

FIG. 5 is an enlarged view of the condensate channel region of FIG. 1, showing a discharge opening at a lower end of a guide duct, the condensate channel, the absorbent wick and its pull tab.

# FIG. 6

## View
Enlarged schematic sectional view, through a wall of the outer shell, of the mechanical exposure indicator, seen horizontally with the indicator stem in the exposed position. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
A thick hatched upright wall body stands across the middle of the drawing area, its outer surface facing left and its inner surface facing right. This wall body is the sectioned outer shell 10.

Carried by the wall body, and drawn as a horizontally elongated plain rectangular outline extending through the thickness of the wall body from its outer surface to its inner surface, is the body of the mechanical exposure indicator 80, shown schematically and open at both of its ends.

An elongated horizontal shaft lies within that outline and extends beyond both of its ends: to the left the shaft projects past the outer surface of the wall body, and to the right its inner end reaches into the open space at the right of the drawing area. This shaft is the indicator stem 82.

A coil spring surrounds the shaft within the outline, drawn as aligned loops and shown extended, its loops spaced apart. This spring is the spring 86.

A small block sits above the shaft within the outline, to the right of the coil spring, projecting downward with its lower end adjacent the upper surface of the shaft, shown schematically. This block is the temperature-responsive latch 84.

In the open space at the right of the drawing area, an upright plain rectangular block is drawn, shown schematically, its left face contacting the inner end of the shaft, so that the two are in thermal contact. This block is the first phase-change cassette 44.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 44, 80, 82, 84, 86

## Numeral targets
- 10: well inside the hatching of the upright wall body, below the indicator outline.
- 44: well inside the upright rectangular block at the right.
- 80: on the outline of the indicator body carried by the wall body, at its left part clear of the shaft.
- 82: on the part of the shaft projecting left beyond the outer surface of the wall body.
- 84: well inside the small block above the shaft.
- 86: on one loop of the coil spring surrounding the shaft.

an insulated lid closable on the upper edge of the outer shell and carrying a depending indexing rib positioned to enter the mating channel as the insulated lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages;

the carrier being free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the outer shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the insulated lid cooperating in the registered position to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through the perforations, and returns through the lower return passage.

content.text:
All eight findings are fixed and the files remain synchronized.

**Geometry defects.** FIG. 6 now shows the cassette face spaced from and thermally coupled to the stem, matching the description's flat "thermally coupled," and states that the spacer frame wall, the guide duct and the side supply passage lying between the shell wall and the cassette are omitted from the schematic detail. FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 now close the bypass: the lower edge of each tray wall meets the floor just inboard of the trough, so the side gap communicates with the space beneath the tray bottom wall only through the openings in that wall, which is the path claims 1, 13 and 17 recite. FIG. 1 also gives the module an upwardly open groove beneath the depending rib that receives the rib's lower end, so the closed state it depicts is the registered state the description requires.

**Claim and description alignment.** Claims 7 and 16 now recite discharge openings, separate from the peripheral outlet openings, at the lower ends of the guide ducts, and the description carries the same relationship in the same words. The condensate channel is now described as a shallow upwardly open trough formed in the outer shell and extending around the product tray, with the channel and wick remaining in the shell when the tray is removed, which is the support claims 16 and 19 need for "a condensate channel of the outer shell."

**Numeral and text corrections.** Numeral 10 is now targeted by a lead line and arrow to the outer shell as a whole in both FIG. 1 and FIG. 6, and FIG. 6 identifies its sectioned wall body as one of the side walls 14, with 14 added to that sheet's numeral list and target. The description no longer narrows the conditioned cassettes to payload-specific conditioning or adds exchange between shipments, in either the thermal module section or Operation. FIG. 2 states that the matching opening in the far long side wall is hidden in that view and not drawn, and the Brief Description of FIG. 2 now says a peripheral outlet opening.

All six briefs are under the character ceiling, no sheet carries more than eight numerals, the numeral table is unchanged with every numeral used and drawn, and the claim set remains 20 claims depending only on claims 1, 6, 9, 13 and 17.

input.summary: Fixed all eight findings. FIG. 6 now shows the cassette spaced from and thermally coupled to the stem and states which intervening structure the detail omits; FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 close the tray skirt onto the floor so air reaches the lower return passage only through the perforations; FIG. 1 gives the module a groove that receives the depending rib; claims 7 and 16 and the description now distinguish the discharge openings from the peripheral outlet openings; the description states that the condensate channel is formed in the outer shell and remains there when the tray is removed; numeral 10 is retargeted to the shell as a whole in FIGS. 1 and 6 with numeral 14 added to FIG. 6; the payload-specific conditioning and inter-shipment exchange wording is removed; and FIG. 2's second outlet opening is resolved as hidden and not drawn, with the Brief Description of FIG. 2 changed to the singular.
reasoning: The two geometry defects were cured in the figure briefs, leaving the claims and description untouched, because the authority runs from the text to the drawing. FIG. 6 now says the cassette face is spaced from and thermally coupled to the stem, which is exactly what the description and claim 9 recite, and it declares that the spacer frame wall, the guide duct and the side supply passage between the shell wall and the cassette are omitted from the schematic detail, so the sheet no longer implies that a cassette abuts the shell interior.

The bypass finding was the more serious one, because as briefed the descending stream could pass under the tray skirt and never cross the perforations, defeating the path in claims 1, 13 and 17. FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 now bring the lower edge of each tray wall down onto the floor just inboard of the trough, so the only communication between the side gap and the space beneath the tray bottom wall is through the openings in that wall. That agrees with FIG. 4, which already put the perforations below the tray bottom wall.

FIG. 1 depicts the closed carrier, so the rib had to have somewhere to seat. Adding an upwardly open groove in the module top surface beneath the rib, with the rib's lower end received in it, makes the parent view show the registered engagement that FIG. 3 enlarges. The groove is left unnumbered on FIG. 1 because numeral 56 is carried on FIGS. 2 and 3.

Claims 7 and 16 previously identified the condensate openings by the same location claim 1 gives the peripheral outlet openings, so the two could not be told apart. # FIG. 1

## View
Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material, all line work inside the drawing area.

## Geometry to draw
Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body form an upright container, open at the top. These are the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body being the floor 12. A block projects inward from each wall body below its top end.

A thick hatched horizontal slab across the top ends of both wall bodies is the insulated lid 60, closed. A narrow rib projects downward from its underside inboard of the left wall body top end, and a small compressible body lies between the slab and each top end.

Inside the container, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched upright walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the floor 12 and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side. Small openings pass through each upright wall below the bottom wall level, and each upright wall stops short of the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12 are the tray feet 22. The open space between that bottom wall and the floor 12 is the lower return passage 24. A shallow upwardly open trough in the floor 12 at the foot of each gap holds an elongated absorbent body.

Between the open top of the product tray 20 and the lid 60 underside, an elongated hatched body drawn in section is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it, spaced from one another and from its ends. The body is open downward at its centre, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the gap. An upwardly open groove in its top surface receives the lower end of the narrow rib.

Three thin broken-line closed curves, without hatching, enclose the upper left region with the rib, groove and left wall body top; the lower left region with the outboard channel opening, the left gap and the tray openings; and the region with the trough and absorbent body. They indicate the regions enlarged in FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 respectively.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

## Numeral targets
- 10: outside the container, with a lead line and arrow to the outer shell as a whole.
- 12: well inside the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left upright wall of the box.
- 22: inside the left short block.
- 24: inside the open space beneath the tray bottom wall.
- 40: outside the container, with a lead line and arrow to the module as a whole.
- 60: well inside the slab at the top.
- 100: outside the container, with a lead line and arrow to the whole carrier.

# FIG. 1

## View
Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material, all line work inside the drawing area.

## Geometry to draw
Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body form an upright container, open at the top. These are the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body being the floor 12. A block projects inward from each wall body below its top end.

A thick hatched horizontal slab across the top ends of both wall bodies is the insulated lid 60, closed. A narrow rib projects downward from its underside inboard of the left wall body top end, and a small compressible body lies between the slab and each top end.

Inside the container, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched upright walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the floor 12 and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side. Small openings pass through each upright wall below the bottom wall level, and each upright wall stops short of the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12 are the tray feet 22. The open space between that bottom wall and the floor 12 is the lower return passage 24. A shallow upwardly open trough in the floor 12 at the foot of each gap holds an elongated absorbent body.

Between the open top of the product tray 20 and the lid 60 underside, an elongated hatched body drawn in section is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it, spaced from one another and from its ends. The body is open downward at its centre, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the gap. An upwardly open groove in its top surface receives the lower end of the narrow rib.

Three thin broken-line closed curves, without hatching, enclose the upper left region with the rib, groove and left wall body top; the lower left region with the outboard channel opening, the left gap and the tray openings; and the region with the trough and absorbent body. They indicate the regions enlarged in FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 respectively.

# FIG. 4

## View
Enlarged view of a lower side region of FIG. 1, seen horizontally in section. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area and runs the full height of the fragment, its inner surface facing right.

In the upper right part of the drawing area, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section. Its left face is spaced from the inner surface of the upright wall body, leaving an open vertical space between them. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50.

At the foot of that channel, an opening passes through the left face of the body fragment, so that the channel opens sideways into the open vertical space between the fragment and the upright wall body. This opening is one of the peripheral outlet openings 54.

Below the body fragment, and spaced to the right of the inner surface of the upright wall body, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section and runs downward to the lower edge of the fragment. This thin wall is one of the tray side walls 26. The open vertical space continues down between the upright wall body and the thin wall, so that the space fed through the peripheral outlet opening 54 runs downward past the thin wall. This continuing space is one of the side supply passages 28.

A thin hatched horizontal bottom wall joins the thin upright wall and extends rightward, and the open space beneath that bottom wall is the lower return passage 24.

In the portion of the thin upright wall below that bottom wall, a series of small openings passes through it, so that the side supply passage 28 opens through them into the space beneath the bottom wall. These openings are the perforations 30.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
24, 26, 28, 30, 50, 54
